slot.brief: Give hydrolysis products of covalent halides such as NCl3 and PCl3/PCl5 and ask why they differ; combine the correct product sets and reasoning in one option set.

stem: On complete hydrolysis, which option gives the products of $\text{NCl}_3$, $\text{PCl}_3$ and $\text{PCl}_5$, respectively, with the correct explanation of their difference?
options: $\text{NH}_3+3\text{HOCl};\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3+3\text{HCl};\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+5\text{HCl}$. The $\text{N–Cl}$ bond is polarised towards N, unlike the $\text{P–Cl}$ bond; phosphorus forms $\text{P–O}$ bonds on hydrolysis.
$\text{NH}_3+3\text{HCl};\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3+3\text{HCl};\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+5\text{HCl}$. All three compounds simply give HCl on hydrolysis.
$\text{NH}_3+3\text{HOCl};\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3+3\text{HCl};\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+5\text{HCl}$. Nitrogen expands its octet during hydrolysis, whereas phosphorus does not.
$\text{NH}_3+3\text{HOCl};\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+3\text{HCl};\ \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3+5\text{HCl}$. The phosphorus oxidation states decrease during hydrolysis.

verdicts.working: The hydrolysis products are NH3 + 3HOCl; H3PO3 + 3HCl; and H3PO4 + 5HCl, so only A and C have the correct products. On the standard Pauling scale, Cl is more electronegative than N, contrary to A’s polarity claim; C’s octet explanation is also false.
issues: A’s claim that the N–Cl bond is polarized toward N is contrary to standard Pauling electronegativities (Cl 3.16, N 3.04); the claim can depend on the electronegativity scale, which is unspecified.
C incorrectly says nitrogen expands its octet during hydrolysis. No option gives both correct products and an unambiguous correct explanation.

verdicts.working: NCl3 + 3H2O -> NH3 + 3HOCl (N is the negative end of N–Cl, so N gets H and Cl gets OH). PCl3 + 3H2O -> H3PO3 + 3HCl and PCl5 + 4H2O -> H3PO4 + 5HCl (P is the positive end, so P forms P–OH bonds, Cl leaves as HCl). All equations balance. Option A has correct products and correct rationale. B has wrong NCl3 products; C has correct products but a false explanation (N cannot expand its octet); D swaps the phosphorus acids and claims reduction, but hydrolysis is not redox.

working:
$\text{NCl}_3+3\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{NH}_3+3\text{HOCl}$
$\text{PCl}_3+3\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3+3\text{HCl}$
$\text{PCl}_5+4\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightarrow\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+5\text{HCl}$
$\text{N}^{\delta-}\! -\!\text{Cl}^{\delta+};\quad \text{P}^{\delta+}\! -\!\text{Cl}^{\delta-}$

Independent check: NCl3 + 3H2O -> NH3 + 3HOCl (N is the negative end of N–Cl, so N gets H and Cl gets OH). PCl3 + 3H2O -> H3PO3 + 3HCl and PCl5 + 4H2O -> H3PO4 + 5HCl (P is the positive end, so P forms P–OH bonds, Cl leaves as HCl). All equations balance. Option A has correct products and correct rationale. B has wrong NCl3 products; C has correct products but a false explanation (N cannot expand its octet); D swaps the phosphorus acids and claims reduction, but hydrolysis is not redox.
solution:
In $\text{NCl}_3$, N is $\text{N}^{4-}$, so hydrolysis gives $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{HOCl}$; in phosphorus chlorides, P is $\text{P}^{4+}$ and forms P–O bonds.
$$
\text{NCl}_3+3\text{H}_2\text{O}\to\text{NH}_3+3\text{HOCl};\quad \text{PCl}_3+3\text{H}_2\text{O}\to\text{H}_3\text{PO}_3+3\text{HCl};\quad \text{PCl}_5+4\text{H}_2\text{O}\to\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4+5\text{HCl}.
$$
Thus the products and bond-polarity explanation match (A).
